claims.claim: One of the major effects of the acceleration was to decrease the time taken to close the gap between the cat and the obstacle for a given DTC or TTC.
claims.source: One of the major effects of the acceleration was to decrease the time taken to close the gap between the cat and the obstacle for a given DTC or TTC.
claims.evidence: This describes the effect of obstacle acceleration on gap closure dynamics.

claims.claim: The acceleration produced major changes in the organization of the sequence of steps prior to the step over the obstacle.
claims.source: This acceleration, which we always applied during the visual dissociation task, produced major changes in the organization of the sequence of steps prior to the step over the obstacle, as illustrated in Figure 7A,B.
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral effect of obstacle acceleration, shown in Figure 7A,B.

claims.claim: In all cases, the acceleration produced a change in the sequence of steps such that the limb that stepped over the obstacle was the opposite of that predicted on the basis of the unperturbed sequence.
claims.source: In particular, in all cases, the acceleration produced a change in the sequence of steps such that the limb that stepped over the obstacle was the opposite of that predicted on the basis of the unperturbed sequence.
claims.evidence: This describes the consistent effect of acceleration on limb selection.

claims.claim: For the example DTC-related cell, cell discharge in the unperturbed visual dissociation task began 745 ms before the step over the obstacle and at a DTC of 30.6 cm.
claims.source: In the example illustrated in Figure 7C (same DTC-related cell as in Figure 3), cell discharge in the unperturbed visual dissociation task (green trace) began 745 ms before the step over the obstacle and at a DTC of 30.6 cm.
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative data for the example cell in the unperturbed condition.

claims.claim: In the acceleration task, the acceleration was applied when the obstacle was 39.4 cm from the cat.
claims.source: In the acceleration task, we applied the acceleration in step −3 of the coBr (orange box), when the obstacle was 39.4 cm from the cat.
claims.evidence: This specifies the distance at which acceleration was applied.

claims.claim: As the obstacle accelerated toward the cat, the example DTC-related cell started to discharge at a DTC of 30.2 cm.
claims.source: As the obstacle accelerated toward the cat, the cell started to discharge at a DTC of 30.2 cm.
claims.evidence: This shows that the DTC-related cell maintained a constant DTC during acceleration.

claims.claim: Because of the acceleration, the example DTC-related cell discharge occurred only 403 ms before the cat stepped over the obstacle.
claims.source: However, because of the acceleration, this discharge occurred only 403 ms before the cat stepped over the obstacle, resulting in the relative delay of the onset of cell discharge in the acceleration task (purple trace) compared to the visual dissociation task (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This shows that the time to step over changed due to acceleration while DTC remained constant.

claims.claim: The projection of the average cell onset in the three tasks onto the DTC traces confirms that the discharge in all three tasks occurred at the same DTC for the example DTC-related cell.
claims.source: However, the projection of the average cell onset in the three tasks (vertical lines) onto the DTC traces confirms that the discharge in all three tasks occurred at the same DTC (see values at top left of Figure 7C: DTC).
claims.evidence: This confirms the DTC-related nature of the example cell across all tasks.

claims.claim: The projection of the average cell onset onto the TTC trace shows that cell onset varied between the three tasks for the example DTC-related cell.
claims.source: In contrast, the projection onto the TTC trace shows that cell onset varied between the three tasks.
claims.evidence: This confirms that TTC varied for the DTC-related cell across tasks.

claims.claim: The constant relationship with DTC for the example neuron held also for the 2R acceleration condition.
claims.source: The constant relationship with DTC for this neuron held also for the 2R acceleration condition as illustrated in Figure 7D.
claims.evidence: This shows that the DTC relationship is maintained across different acceleration conditions.

claims.claim: An acceleration occurring prior to the predicted time of onset and the predicted DTC did not modify the onset of the cell discharge for the example DTC-related cell.
claims.source: Therefore, an acceleration occurring prior to the predicted time of onset and the predicted DTC did not modify the onset of the cell discharge.
claims.evidence: This shows that early accelerations do not affect DTC-related cell discharge onset.

claims.claim: Most cells displayed similar changes in activity to those illustrated in Figure 7 in response to acceleration of the obstacle.
claims.source: Most cells displayed similar changes in activity to those illustrated in Figure 7 in response to acceleration of the obstacle.
claims.evidence: This generalizes the acceleration response to the broader cell population.

claims.claim: The onset of cell discharge during the 1L condition of the acceleration task was delayed with respect to onset during the visual dissociation task for the vast majority (33/36) of cells tested.
claims.source: The onset of cell discharge during the 1L condition of the acceleration task was delayed with respect to onset during the visual dissociation task for the vast majority (33/36) of cells tested in this condition (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of 1L acceleration on cell discharge onset, shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: A significant delay in cell onset was found in 19/36 cells during the 1L acceleration condition.
claims.source: We found a significant delay in 19/36 of these cells (t-tests, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the delay in cell onset during 1L acceleration.

claims.claim: Cell onset was relatively delayed for most (8/9) cells following acceleration in the 1R condition.
claims.source: Cell onset was also relatively delayed for most (8/9) cells following acceleration in the 1R condition and was significant in 2/9 cells (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of 1R acceleration on cell discharge onset.

claims.claim: The onset of discharge activity was less frequently delayed in the 2L and the 2R conditions, with significant differences in only 1/9 and 2/26 cells, respectively.
claims.source: However, the onset of discharge activity was less frequently delayed in the 2L and the 2R conditions, in which we found significant differences in only 1/9 and 2/26 cells, respectively (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of 2L and 2R accelerations on cell discharge onset, shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Acceleration was less likely to modify the onset of cell discharge the earlier it was applied.
claims.source: In general, acceleration was less likely to modify the onset of cell discharge the earlier we applied it.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the relationship between acceleration timing and its effect on cell discharge.

claims.claim: In the majority of cases, the onset of cell discharge maintained a constant relationship to either distance or time when accelerations were included in the analysis.
claims.source: We found that in the majority of cases, the onset of cell discharge maintained a constant relationship to either distance (e.g. Figure 5A) or time (e.g. Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This shows that the DTC/TTC relationships are robust to acceleration perturbations.

claims.claim: For 8 of 14 cells showing a relationship to DTC, 20 acceleration conditions could be tested, and in most of these (18/20), the relationship with DTC was maintained during the different acceleration conditions.
claims.source: We could test 20 acceleration conditions for 8/14 cells showing a relationship to DTC, and in most of these (18/20), the relationship with DTC was maintained during the different acceleration conditions (7/9, 1L; 2/2, 1R; 3/3, 2L; 6/6, 2R).
claims.evidence: This quantifies how well DTC-related cells maintained their relationship during accelerations.

claims.claim: For 8 of 15 cells with a constant relationship to TTC, 25 acceleration conditions were tested, and most (16/25) maintained this relationship with the accelerations.
claims.source: Similarly, we tested 25 acceleration conditions for 8/15 cells with a constant relationship to TTC and most (16/25) equally maintained this relationship with the accelerations (6/11, 1L; 5/5, 1R; 1/1, 2L; 4/8, 2R).
claims.evidence: This quantifies how well TTC-related cells maintained their relationship during accelerations.

claims.claim: Most cells showed a marked increase in the slope of the increase in discharge frequency during the acceleration, particularly during the 1L condition.
claims.source: Importantly, most cells showed a marked increase in the slope of the increase in discharge frequency during the acceleration, particularly during the 1L condition (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: This describes a key change in cell discharge dynamics during acceleration, shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: Three quarters of the examples (49/67, 73%) showed an increase in the slope of the activity during the acceleration.
claims.source: Altogether, three quarters of our examples (49/67, 73%) showed an increase in the slope of the activity during the acceleration.
claims.evidence: This quantifies the prevalence of increased discharge slope during acceleration.

claims.claim: The largest changes in slope were observed in the 1L and 2R conditions.
claims.source: We observed the largest changes in slope in the 1L and 2R conditions.
claims.evidence: This identifies which acceleration conditions produced the greatest changes in discharge slope.

claims.claim: The slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 3.3 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 1L condition.
claims.source: These population plots show that the slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 3.3 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 1L condition and 2.9 times greater in the 2R condition.
claims.evidence: This quantifies the increase in population discharge slope during 1L acceleration.

claims.claim: The slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 2.9 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 2R condition.
claims.source: These population plots show that the slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 3.3 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 1L condition and 2.9 times greater in the 2R condition.
claims.evidence: This quantifies the increase in population discharge slope during 2R acceleration.

claims.claim: No noticeable change in the slope of the discharge was observed for the 2L condition.
claims.source: However, we did not observe any noticeable change in the slope of the discharge for the 2L condition (see Figure 9—figure supplement 1B), in which the acceleration occurred earlier (average of 1608 ms) than the onset of discharge activity in most cells.
claims.evidence: This describes the lack of slope change for early accelerations (2L condition).

claims.claim: The increased slope of the discharge in conditions where acceleration relatively delayed cell onset likely provides information on the rate of change of gap closure.
claims.source: It is probable that the increased slope of the discharge in the conditions in which the acceleration relatively delayed cell onset provides information on the rate of change of gap closure (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This interprets the functional significance of the increased discharge slope.

claims.claim: The cells in the study did not discharge purely to the visual stimulus.
claims.source: However, the cells in our study did not discharge purely to the visual stimulus, in which case they might have been expected to discharge throughout the period that the obstacle was visible (10–12 steps before the step over the obstacle).
claims.evidence: This argues against a purely visual response interpretation of the cell discharge.

claims.claim: The cells began to discharge only when the obstacle was at a fixed DTC or TTC from the cat.
claims.source: Rather, they began to discharge only when the obstacle was at a fixed DTC or TTC from the cat.
claims.evidence: This describes the tuning of cell responses to specific DTC or TTC values.

claims.claim: Most of the cells maintained their relationship to DTC or TTC even when the obstacle was accelerated toward the cat.
claims.source: Moreover, most of the cells maintained this relationship even when we accelerated the obstacle toward the cat.
claims.evidence: This demonstrates the robustness of the DTC/TTC relationships.

claims.claim: The cells are tuned to respond to objects only when they are within a limited range of DTC or TTC.
claims.source: This suggests that these cells are tuned to respond to objects only when they are within a limited range of DTC or TTC.
claims.evidence: This interprets the selectivity of cell responses.

claims.claim: A similar tuning of cell responses to distance in response to looming stimuli is found in the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) of the PPC in non-human primates.
claims.source: A similar tuning of cell responses to distance in response to looming stimuli is found in the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) of the PPC in non-human primates (Colby et al., 1993; Graziano and Cooke, 2006; see also Hadjidimitrakis et al., 2015), as well as in the premotor cortex (PMC, Graziano et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This references similar findings in primate studies.

claims.claim: Graziano has proposed that cells tuned to distance may play a role in defensive and avoidance behavior.
claims.source: Graziano (Graziano and Cooke, 2006) has proposed that such cells may play a role in defensive and avoidance behavior.
claims.evidence: This references a proposed functional role for distance-tuned cells.

claims.claim: The discharge activity should be considered in the context of a coordinated and planned motor activity rather than simply in terms of the visual stimulus.
claims.source: The discharge activity should therefore not be considered simply in terms of the visual stimulus but rather in the context of a coordinated and planned motor activity.
claims.evidence: This proposes an interpretation of the cell discharge as motor-related rather than purely sensory.

claims.claim: Cells responding at fixed DTC and TTC might be considered as providing important context-dependent information that is used to plan the upcoming gait modification.
claims.source: In this respect, cells responding at fixed DTC and TTC might be considered as providing important context-dependent information that is used to plan the upcoming gait modification.
claims.evidence: This proposes a functional role for the DTC and TTC cells in motor planning.

claims.claim: The cells discharged in a staggered manner over a limited range of DTC and TTC.
claims.source: Moreover, as in the experiments referenced above with respect to the VIP and PMC, the cells in our study discharged in a staggered manner over a limited range of DTC and TTC.
claims.evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of cell activation across the population.

claims.claim: The staggered discharge feature would provide a means for animals to continually monitor the rate of gap closure over the range in which a gait modification needs to be planned.
claims.source: We believe that this feature of the discharge activity would provide a means for animals to continually monitor the rate of gap closure over the range in which a gait modification needs to be planned.
claims.evidence: This proposes a functional interpretation of the staggered discharge pattern.

claims.claim: The ability to continually monitor obstacle location over time would facilitate the detection of any non-linearities in the rate of gap closure.
claims.source: The ability to continually monitor obstacle location over time would facilitate the detection of any non-linearities in the rate of gap closure and might be particularly important in helping the cats negotiate the obstacle when it is accelerated.
claims.evidence: This proposes a functional advantage of continuous monitoring.

claims.claim: In a more natural situation, the sequential activation of both DTC and TTC-related cells would be necessary for estimating the gap with a prey moving at unpredictable speeds.
claims.source: In a more natural situation, the sequential activation of both DTC and TTC-related cells would be necessary for estimating the gap with a prey moving at unpredictable speeds, different from those of the predator.
claims.evidence: This proposes an ecological function for the two cell populations.

claims.claim: Although the cells discharged at fixed DTC/TTC before the gait modification, cell discharge continued until the step over the obstacle.
claims.source: It is important to emphasize that although the cells discharged at fixed DTC/TTC before the gait modification, cell discharge continued until the step over the obstacle.
claims.evidence: This describes the sustained nature of cell discharge.

claims.claim: The increased discharge prior to the step over the obstacle is not a pure visual response but rather represents the starting point of a complex sensorimotor transformation involved in planning the gait modification.
claims.source: As such, we believe that the increased discharge prior to the step over the obstacle is not a pure visual response but rather represents the starting point of a complex sensorimotor transformation involved in planning the gait modification.
claims.evidence: This proposes an interpretation of the cell discharge as part of sensorimotor transformation.

claims.claim: Visual input is essential for initiating the sensorimotor transformation, but once initiated planning can continue in the absence of continual visual input.
claims.source: In this view, visual input is essential for initiating the sensorimotor transformation, but once initiated planning can continue in the absence of continual visual input.
claims.evidence: This proposes a model for how visual information is used in motor planning.

claims.claim: Lesion of the PPC region results in a marked locomotor deficit defined by an inability to appropriately place the plant limb in front of the obstacle.
claims.source: Lesion of the PPC region in which we recorded these cells results in a marked locomotor deficit defined by an inability to appropriately place the plant limb in front of the obstacle (Lajoie and Drew, 2007).
claims.evidence: This references lesion study results supporting a functional role for the PPC.

claims.claim: The deficit from PPC lesions is indicative of an error in planning rather than one of perception or action.
claims.source: We have previously discussed the reasons that we believe that this deficit is indicative of an error in planning rather than one of perception or action.
claims.evidence: This interprets the nature of the deficit from PPC lesions.

claims.claim: In the absence of information about the relative location of the obstacle and of the rate of gap closure provided by the cells in the PPC, the cat is unable to determine where to position its leg in front of the obstacle and when to start the gait modification.
claims.source: We propose that in the absence of information about the relative location of the obstacle and of the rate of gap closure provided by the cells in the PPC, the cat is unable to determine where to position its leg in front of the obstacle and when to start the gait modification.
claims.evidence: This proposes a functional interpretation of the lesion deficit.

claims.claim: The ensemble activity of the population of cells demonstrates a progressive increase in discharge rate up to the time of the gait modification.
claims.source: The ensemble activity of the population of cells demonstrates a progressive increase in discharge rate up to the time of the gait modification.
claims.evidence: This describes the population-level discharge pattern.

claims.claim: A similar ramp increase in cell discharge as TTC progressively decreases has been observed in the motor cortex in monkeys trained to intercept a simulated object with their arm.
claims.source: A similar ramp increase in cell discharge as TTC progressively decreases has been observed in the motor cortex in monkeys trained to intercept a simulated object with their arm (Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006).
claims.evidence: This references similar findings in primate motor cortex.

claims.claim: The ramp increase in the population discharge provides a signal that indicates the imminent requirement to make the gait modification.
claims.source: In our task, we propose that this ramp increase in the population discharge provides a signal that indicates the imminent requirement to make the gait modification.
claims.evidence: This proposes a functional interpretation of the ramp discharge.

claims.claim: The ramp discharge is reminiscent of that observed in several structures and in many tasks in which motor activity is self-initiated.
claims.source: This ramp discharge is reminiscent of that observed in several structures and in many tasks in which motor activity is self-initiated (Lebedev et al., 2008; Maimon and Assad, 2006a, 2006b; Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006) and is particularly prevalent in tasks in which a decision to move on the basis of ambiguous or delayed information is required (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005; Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Thura and Cisek, 2014).
claims.evidence: This references similar ramp discharge patterns in other contexts.

claims.claim: Thura and Cisek (2014) refer to the time at which a decision is made as the time of commitment.
claims.source: Thura and Cisek (2014) refer to the time at which such a decision is made as the time of commitment.
claims.evidence: This references a concept from decision-making literature.

claims.claim: The peak of activity in the population of cells indicates a time of commitment, at which point the cat initiates the gait modification.
claims.source: We consider that the peak of activity in our population of cells also indicates a time of commitment, at which point the cat initiates the gait modification.
claims.evidence: This proposes an interpretation of the peak discharge as a commitment signal.

claims.claim: When the obstacle was accelerated, a greater slope of the activity was found between the onset of cell discharge and the onset of the gait modification than in the absence of acceleration.
claims.source: In this respect, it is pertinent that when we accelerated the obstacle, we found a greater slope of the activity between the onset of cell discharge and the onset of the gait modification than in the absence of acceleration.
claims.evidence: This describes a key finding about discharge dynamics during acceleration.

claims.claim: The increased slope during acceleration allowed the cells to reach a similar peak value in the shorter time available to the cat to make the gait modification.
claims.source: This increased slope allowed the cells to reach a similar peak value in the shorter time available to the cat to make the gait modification.
claims.evidence: This interprets the functional significance of the increased slope during acceleration.

claims.claim: The discharge is limb-independent, that is, it is identical regardless of whether the left or the right limb is the first to step over the obstacle.
claims.source: Although we believe that the activity that we observed in this task forms part of the sensorimotor transformation that leads to the gait modification, its function has to be discussed in light of the fact that the discharge is limb-independent, that is, it is identical regardless of whether the left or the right limb is the first to step over the obstacle.
claims.evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the recorded neurons.

claims.claim: One study suggests that activity in the PPC is not expressed until the effector limb has been specified, and then only for the contralateral limb.
claims.source: This is contrary to one study (Bernier et al., 2012) that suggests that activity in the PPC is not expressed until the effector limb has been specified, and then only for the contralateral limb (although see Chang et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: This references a contrasting finding from another study.

claims.claim: The nature of the task requirements is probably the main determinant of whether PPC activity is limb-dependent or limb-independent.
claims.source: While this disparity could relate to species or area-specific differences, we believe that the nature of the task requirements is probably the main determinant.
claims.evidence: This proposes an explanation for differences between studies.

claims.claim: In the experiments of Bernier et al. (2012), subjects were static and an external cue specified the arm to move.
claims.source: In the experiments of Bernier et al. (2012), subjects were static and an external cue specified the arm to move.
claims.evidence: This describes the task conditions in a contrasting study.

claims.claim: In the current task, the cat is walking and the leg that will step over the obstacle is not pre-defined.
claims.source: In our task, the cat is walking and the leg that will step over the obstacle is not pre-defined.
claims.evidence: This describes a key difference in the current task design.

claims.claim: The decision as to which limb to use to step over the obstacle should be viewed as an emergent property of the task rather than as an instructed movement or a decision made in advance of the movement.
claims.source: As such, we suggest that the decision as to which limb to use to step over the obstacle should be viewed as an emergent property of the task rather than as an instructed movement or a decision made in advance of the movement as in the tasks referenced above.
claims.evidence: This proposes an interpretation of limb selection in the current task.

claims.claim: Information on gap closure could be used to initiate a gait modification through integration with a signal that provides information on the state of the limb.
claims.source: One possible manner in which information on gap closure could be used to initiate a gait modification is illustrated in Figure 10. In this conceptual model, we presume that there is an integration of the gap closure signal with a second signal that provides information on the state of the limb.
claims.evidence: This proposes a conceptual model for how gap closure information is used, illustrated in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The integration with limb state ensures that the gait modification will only be initiated when the limb is in the appropriate state.
claims.source: The integration with limb state ensures that the gait modification will only be initiated when the limb is in the appropriate state, that is, at the end of the stance phase and ready to initiate the transfer of the limb over the obstacle.
claims.evidence: This explains the proposed function of integrating gap closure with limb state.

claims.claim: The integration of gap closure and limb state signals proceeds bilaterally and the limb selected to be the first to step over the obstacle depends on which side wins the competition.
claims.source: We propose that this integration proceeds bilaterally and the limb selected to be the first to step over the obstacle depends on which side wins the competition.
claims.evidence: This proposes a bilateral competition model for limb selection.

claims.claim: All of the cells recorded in this study were located in layer V and therefore project to subcortical structures, including the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
claims.source: Although we do not wish to unduly speculate on where this integration would occur, we would note that all of the cells recorded in this study were located in layer V and therefore project to subcortical structures, including the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This describes the anatomical location and projection targets of the recorded neurons.

claims.claim: The results provide new insights, at the single cell level, into the sensorimotor transformations that underlie the control of visually guided walking.
claims.source: In conclusion, our results provide new insights, at the single cell level, into the sensorimotor transformations that underlie the control of visually guided walking.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the contribution of the study.

claims.claim: The demonstration of populations of cells that can serve to provide information on gap closure and potentially initiate precise gait changes is a novel contribution to understanding the control mechanisms used to guide locomotion.
claims.source: The demonstration of populations of cells that can serve to provide information on gap closure and potentially initiate precise gait changes is a novel contribution to our understanding of the control mechanisms used to guide locomotion.
claims.evidence: This emphasizes the novelty of the findings.

claims.claim: The PPC may have a privileged position in contributing to the ability to plan the gait adjustments needed to negotiate a complex environment.
claims.source: Taken together with the results from studies in various species that show a contribution of the PPC to spatial navigation (Calton and Taube, 2009; Harvey et al., 2012; Whitlock, 2014), it is possible that the PPC may have a privileged position in contributing to our ability to plan the gait adjustments needed to negotiate a complex environment.
claims.evidence: This proposes a broader functional role for the PPC in locomotor control.

claims.claim: Cats were trained to walk on a treadmill at a constant speed of 0.45 m.s−1.
claims.source: We initially trained the cats to walk on a treadmill at a constant speed of 0.45 m.s−1 (unobstructed locomotion) and then trained them to step over obstacles attached to a second belt that moved at the same speed as the treadmill (matched task).
claims.evidence: This describes the training protocol.

claims.claim: Cats very rarely, if ever, hit the obstacle, even in conditions in which the acceleration occurred just before the planned gait modification.
claims.source: Note that cats very rarely, if ever, hit the obstacle, even in conditions in which the acceleration occurred just before the planned gait modification.
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral performance of the cats.

claims.claim: Two obstacles (cylindrical in shape and each of 10 cm cross-section), separated by 3 m, were attached to the treadmill belt.
claims.source: Two obstacles (cylindrical in shape and each of 10 cm cross-section), separated by 3 m, were attached to the treadmill belt.
claims.evidence: This describes the obstacle configuration.

claims.claim: The cat generally made 12–14 steps (6–7 step cycles) between each obstacle.
claims.source: Depending on the speed of the treadmill, the cat generally made 12–14 steps (6–7 step cycles) between each obstacle.
claims.evidence: This describes the step pattern between obstacles.

claims.claim: The obstacle became visible to the cat ~2 m before the step over the obstacle.
claims.source: The obstacle became visible to the cat ~2 m before the step over the obstacle.
claims.evidence: This specifies when the obstacle became visible.

claims.claim: The obstacle was visible to the cat for 5–7 s before the gait modification, during which time the cat made 10–12 steps.
claims.source: The obstacle was therefore visible to the cat for 5–7 s before the gait modification, during which time the cat made 10–12 steps.
claims.evidence: This describes the duration of obstacle visibility.

claims.claim: All handling and surgical procedures followed the recommendations of the Canadian Council for the Protection of Animals.
claims.source: All handling and surgical procedures followed the recommendations of the Canadian Council for the Protection of Animals, and the animal ethics committee at the Université de Montréal approved the experimental protocols (#12_082).
claims.evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claims.claim: A stainless steel baseplate was placed over the right PPC based on an MRI taken 1–2 weeks before the surgery.
claims.source: In brief, based on an MRI taken 1–2 weeks before the surgery, we placed a stainless steel baseplate (internal dimensions = 12 by 6 mm) over the right PPC and then formed a recording chamber around it with dental acrylic.
claims.evidence: This describes the surgical preparation for recordings.

claims.claim: Pairs of Teflon-insulated, stainless steel braided wires were implanted into selected fore- and hindlimb muscles to record electromyographic (EMG) activity.
claims.source: We implanted pairs of Teflon-insulated, stainless steel braided wires into selected fore- and hindlimb muscles to record electromyographic (EMG) activity.
claims.evidence: This describes the EMG recording method.

claims.claim: Microwires were inserted into the cerebral peduncle to allow for antidromic identification of projection neurons in layer V of the PPC.
claims.source: To allow for antidromic identification of projection neurons in layer V of the PPC, we inserted microwires into the cerebral peduncle by using a harpoon assembly (Drew, 1993; Palmer, 1978).
claims.evidence: This describes the method for identifying layer V neurons.

claims.claim: Experiments started 1 week after the surgery.
claims.source: Experiments started 1 week after the surgery.
claims.evidence: This specifies the recovery period before experiments began.

claims.claim: A conventional glass-insulated tungsten microelectrode (0.5–1.5 MΩ) was introduced into the PPC using a custom-made microdrive.
claims.source: In each recording session, we introduced a conventional glass-insulated tungsten microelectrode (0.5–1.5 MΩ) into the PPC using a custom-made microdrive.
claims.evidence: This describes the recording electrode and method.

claims.claim: The electrode was advanced until stimulation of the electrodes in the cerebral peduncle produced antidromic discharges, providing evidence that the electrode had reached layer V.
claims.source: We advanced the electrode until stimulation of the electrodes in the cerebral peduncle produced antidromic discharges either in an isolated unit or in smaller units in the background. This provided evidence that the electrode had reached layer V.
claims.evidence: This describes the method for confirming electrode depth.

claims.claim: Cell activity was recorded from well-isolated single units while the cat walked on the treadmill.
claims.source: We recorded cell activity from well-isolated single units while the cat walked on the treadmill in the matched task until approximately 10 steps over the obstacle with each leg as the lead limb had been made.
claims.evidence: This describes the recording protocol.

claims.claim: Steps in which the obstacle accelerated were interspersed unpredictably with steps where the obstacle continued at its pre-set speed.
claims.source: Steps in which the obstacle accelerated were interspersed unpredictably with steps where the obstacle continued at its pre-set speed.
claims.evidence: This describes the randomization of acceleration trials.

claims.claim: The entire data collection period occupied 15–20 min.
claims.source: The entire data collection period occupied 15–20 min, although we sometimes lost cell stability before we could complete the recording session.
claims.evidence: This specifies the duration of recording sessions.

claims.claim: EMG activity was band-pass filtered at 100–475 Hz and digitized online at a frequency of 1 KHz.
claims.source: We band-pass filtered EMG activity at 100–475 Hz and digitized it online at a frequency of 1 KHz.
claims.evidence: This describes the EMG signal processing.

claims.claim: Cell activity was digitized at a frequency of 100 KHz to discriminate cells offline.
claims.source: To discriminate cells offline, we digitized cell activity at a frequency of 100 KHz.
claims.evidence: This describes the cell recording sampling rate.

claims.claim: A six-camera Vicon motion analysis system recorded, at 100 Hz, the position of light-reflecting points placed on a rod attached to the head of the cat and along the length of each obstacle.
claims.source: In all experiments, a six-camera Vicon motion analysis system recorded, at 100 Hz, the position of light-reflecting points placed on a rod attached to the head of the cat and along the length of each obstacle.

results.result: Two distinct populations of neurons in the PPC (primarily area 5b) were identified: 14/51 cells signaled distance-to-contact (DTC) and 15/51 cells signaled time-to-contact (TTC) with an approaching obstacle, regardless of which limb stepped over the obstacle first. These populations were anatomically intermixed throughout area 5b and the 5/7 border region, with both cell types found in each cat.
results.evaluation: The identification of two distinct neuronal populations is well-supported by rigorous statistical analysis (one-way ANOVAs with p<0.01 threshold, C51-C52), clear separation in the modulation index (C58), and validation through bootstrapping (C59). The limb-independence (C5) and anatomical distribution (C55-C57) are documented with appropriate data. The sample size (51 cells analyzed from 67 total) is adequate for the statistical tests performed.

results.result: TTC-related cells discharged when the obstacle was 300-1000 ms away, while DTC-related cells discharged when the obstacle was 20-40 cm away, corresponding to 1-2 steps before the obstacle. The staggered onset of cells within each population resulted in a progressive ramp increase in population discharge activity beginning 2-3 steps before the step over the obstacle.
results.evaluation: The temporal and spatial characteristics of the two cell populations are clearly documented (C60-C61) with appropriate histograms (Figure 5E). The interpretation that these values correspond to 1-2 steps before the obstacle (C62) is reasonable given the experimental parameters. The population-level ramp discharge (C64-C65) is demonstrated in Figure 6 with adequate sample sizes (14 DTC and 15 TTC cells).

results.result: The visual dissociation task successfully dissociated DTC from TTC by slowing obstacle speed to 0.3 m/s while maintaining treadmill speed at 0.45 m/s. For the example DTC-related cell, discharge onset occurred at significantly different times between tasks (514±124 ms in matched vs 745±161 ms in visual dissociation, p<0.001) but at constant DTC, while TTC varied significantly. The opposite pattern was observed for TTC-related cells.
results.evaluation: The experimental design effectively dissociates DTC and TTC (C21-C26), and the quantitative data for example cells are well-documented with appropriate statistics (C33-C38, C43-C48). The t-tests show significant differences (p<0.001 and p=0.002) for the matched vs visual dissociation comparison (C37-C38). The ANOVA results confirm the expected patterns for both DTC-related (C43-C45) and TTC-related (C46-C48) cells. However, the analysis relies heavily on example cells; population-level statistics would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Obstacle acceleration decreased the time to close the gap and consistently reversed the limb sequence. Most cells (18/20 DTC-related and 16/25 TTC-related conditions tested) maintained their relationship to DTC or TTC during acceleration. The onset of cell discharge was delayed during 1L acceleration (33/36 cells, 19/36 significant at p<0.05) but less frequently during earlier accelerations (2L and 2R conditions).
results.evaluation: The acceleration manipulation provides a strong test of the DTC/TTC relationships (C71-C73). The example cell data clearly demonstrate maintained DTC relationships during acceleration (C74-C81). The population analysis shows that most cells maintained their DTC or TTC relationships (C88-C90), though the sample sizes for some acceleration conditions are small (e.g., 2/2 for 1R in DTC cells). The delayed onset during 1L acceleration is well-documented (C83-C84), and the timing-dependent effect (C87) is logical given the experimental design.

results.result: During obstacle acceleration, 73% of cells (49/67) showed increased discharge slope, with the largest changes in 1L and 2R conditions. Population discharge slope increased 3.3-fold during 1L acceleration and 2.9-fold during 2R acceleration compared to unperturbed trials. No slope change was observed for 2L acceleration, where acceleration occurred earlier than typical cell discharge onset.
results.evaluation: The increased discharge slope during acceleration is well-documented at both single-cell (C91) and population levels (C92-C95). The quantification of slope increases (3.3x for 1L, 2.9x for 2R) is specific and appears to be based on population averages shown in Figure 9. The lack of slope change for 2L acceleration (C96) is consistent with the timing of acceleration relative to cell discharge onset. However, the interpretation that increased slope provides information about rate of gap closure (C97, C122-C123) is speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: All analyzed cells were limb-independent, discharging identically regardless of which limb stepped over the obstacle first. Cells were classified as step-advanced (discharge >200 ms before obstacle) rather than step-related, with no relationship between cell discharge onset and muscle activity in the step before the obstacle, but a significant relationship between discharge end and lead limb muscle activity during the step over.
results.evaluation: The limb-independence criterion is clearly defined (C166) and consistently applied as an inclusion criterion (C175). The demonstration that cells are not simply step-related is supported by the lack of correlation with muscle activity in preceding steps (C40) and the significant relationship with lead limb activity during the step over (C41). The generalization to all cells in the database (C42) is appropriate given that limb-independence was an inclusion criterion. The >200 ms threshold for step-advanced classification (C165, C174) is reasonable but somewhat arbitrary.

results.result: The neuronal database consisted of 67 cells from two cats (37 from PCM7, 30 from PCM9), recorded from area 5b and the 5/7 border region, with 43/67 antidromically identified as layer V projection neurons. Cells were selected based on anatomical location, layer V identification, step-advanced discharge (>200 ms before obstacle), limb-independence, and minimum trial numbers (≥5 unperturbed, ≥3 acceleration per condition).
results.evaluation: The database composition is clearly documented (C27-C31) with explicit inclusion criteria (C171-C173, C176). The antidromic identification of 43/67 cells as layer V neurons (C173) provides strong anatomical validation, with the remaining 24 cells recorded adjacent to identified cells. The inclusion criteria are appropriate for the study's goals. However, the sample size of only 2 cats is a limitation for generalizability, though both cats showed similar cell types (C57).

results.result: Population discharge onset occurred earlier in the visual dissociation task than the matched task for DTC-related cells, but at the same time for TTC-related cells. Peak discharge for both populations occurred just before or after the onset of gait modification. An early increase in DTC-related population discharge was observed 5-6 steps before the obstacle in the visual dissociation task, representing a tonic increase rather than an artifact.
results.evaluation: The task-dependent differences in population discharge onset (C66-C67) are consistent with the single-cell findings and clearly shown in Figure 6. The timing of peak discharge relative to gait modification (C68) is well-documented. The early increase in DTC-related discharge (C69-C70) is noted and attributed to a real phenomenon based on Figure 6—figure supplement 1, though the functional significance of this early activity is not explored. The population analyses appropriately combine data from multiple cells.

results.result: Among the 51 cells analyzed, 6/51 showed significant effects of both DTC and TTC, and 16/51 showed non-significant effects of both variables.
results.evaluation: These cells represent those that did not fit cleanly into the DTC or TTC categories based on the statistical criteria (p<0.01). The quantification is straightforward and the cells are appropriately identified in Figure 5C (green and gray squares). However, the functional significance of these cells is not explored, and they appear to be excluded from subsequent population analyses focused on the clearly defined DTC and TTC cells.

results.result: Cells did not discharge purely to visual stimuli but were tuned to respond only when the obstacle was within a limited range of DTC or TTC. Cell discharge continued until the step over the obstacle, representing the starting point of a sensorimotor transformation for planning gait modification rather than a pure visual response.
results.evaluation: The interpretation that cells are not purely visual (C98) is reasonable given that discharge begins at specific DTC/TTC values rather than throughout obstacle visibility. The tuning to limited ranges (C101) is supported by the data in C60-C61. However, the claims about sensorimotor transformation (C104-C105, C111-C112) are interpretations rather than direct demonstrations. The study does not include experiments that would definitively distinguish sensory from motor planning signals, such as trials where visual information is removed or motor output is prevented.

results.result: The staggered discharge pattern across cells would provide a means to continually monitor gap closure rate, facilitate detection of non-linearities in gap closure, and be necessary for estimating gaps with prey moving at unpredictable speeds.
results.evaluation: The staggered discharge pattern is well-documented (C106, supported by C63-C64), but the proposed functions (C107-C109) are speculative. While the interpretation is plausible and consistent with the data, the study does not directly test whether these cells actually monitor gap closure rate or detect non-linearities. The proposal about natural predator-prey situations (C109) is entirely speculative and extends beyond the experimental paradigm. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not demonstrated by the current data.

results.result: Lesions of the PPC region result in an inability to appropriately place the plant limb in front of the obstacle, indicative of a planning error. In the absence of PPC information about obstacle location and gap closure rate, cats cannot determine where to position the leg or when to start the gait modification.
results.evaluation: The lesion data (C113) is cited from prior work (Lajoie and Drew, 2007) rather than presented in this study. While the authors reference their previous discussion of why this represents a planning deficit (C114), the interpretation that the deficit specifically results from loss of DTC/TTC information (C115) is speculative. Lesions are not cell-type specific and would affect all PPC neurons in the region, not just the DTC and TTC cells identified here. The causal link between the specific cell populations described and the lesion deficit is inferred but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The progressive ramp increase in population discharge up to gait modification provides a signal indicating the imminent requirement to modify gait. The peak of activity represents a 'time of commitment' at which the cat initiates the gait modification, similar to ramp discharges observed in self-initiated movements and decision-making tasks.
results.evaluation: The ramp increase in population discharge is well-documented (C116, supported by C64-C65, Figure 6). The comparison to similar phenomena in other motor systems (C117, C119) is appropriate and well-cited. However, the interpretation that this represents a commitment signal (C121) is speculative. The study does not include experiments that would test this hypothesis, such as examining whether the peak discharge timing predicts movement onset variability or whether perturbations after peak discharge still result in gait modification. The analogy to decision-making tasks (C119-C120) is interesting but does not constitute evidence for this specific function.

results.result: The limb-independence of PPC activity differs from one study suggesting limb-specific activity only after effector specification. This disparity likely reflects task differences: in the current task, the cat is walking and the lead limb is not pre-defined, making limb selection an emergent property rather than an instructed movement.
results.evaluation: The observation of limb-independent activity is well-supported by the current data (C124-C125). The comparison to Bernier et al. (2012) is appropriate (C125, C127), and the proposed explanation based on task differences (C126, C128-C129) is plausible. However, this remains speculative without direct experimental comparison. The interpretation that limb selection is an 'emergent property' (C129) is reasonable but not directly tested. Species differences (cat vs. primate) and area differences (5b vs. other PPC regions) could also contribute to the disparity but are not fully explored.

results.result: A conceptual model proposes that gap closure information is integrated with limb state signals bilaterally, with the limb selected to step over the obstacle determined by which side wins the competition. Integration likely occurs in subcortical structures (basal ganglia or cerebellum) that receive projections from layer V PPC neurons.
results.evaluation: This is explicitly presented as a conceptual model (C130) and speculation (C132). While the model is illustrated in Figure 10 and is consistent with the data, it is not tested experimentally. The observation that all recorded cells are in layer V and project subcortically (C133) is supported, but the specific proposal about integration sites is speculative. The model provides a reasonable framework for future experiments but should not be considered a demonstrated result of the current study.

results.result: The PPC contributes to visually guided locomotor gait modifications by constructing an estimation of object location relative to body state. The demonstration of DTC and TTC cell populations provides new insights into sensorimotor transformations underlying visually guided walking, with the PPC potentially having a privileged position in planning gait adjustments for navigating complex environments.
results.evaluation: The main hypothesis (C1) is supported by the identification of DTC and TTC cells, but the claim that these cells 'construct an estimation' is an interpretation rather than a direct demonstration. The study successfully identifies neural correlates of gap closure (C2) and shows they are related to gait modification timing, but the causal role in 'constructing estimations' or 'initiating' gait modifications (C6) is not directly tested. The claims about novelty (C134-C135) are reasonable, but the proposal about the PPC's 'privileged position' (C136) extends beyond the data by citing navigation studies without directly linking those findings to the current results.

results.result: Cats performed the obstacle avoidance task stereotypically, with DTC and TTC decreasing monotonically to ~0 at step onset. The obstacle became visible ~2 m (5-7 s, 10-12 steps) before the gait modification. Cats rarely hit the obstacle, even during late accelerations.
results.evaluation: The behavioral characterization is well-documented with appropriate citations (C19) and clear descriptions of the temporal relationships (C20, C141-C142). The task parameters are precisely specified (C137-C140). The observation that cats rarely hit the obstacle (C138) demonstrates task proficiency and validates the experimental approach. This behavioral foundation is essential for interpreting the neural data.

results.result: Comprehensive methodological details are provided for surgical procedures, recording techniques, data acquisition, spike sorting, EMG analysis, statistical methods, and histological verification of recording locations.
results.evaluation: The methods are described in appropriate detail for reproducibility. Key strengths include: antidromic identification of layer V neurons (C146, C149), high sampling rates for spike discrimination (100 kHz, C154), motion tracking for DTC/TTC calculation (C155, C161), clear statistical criteria (C167-C169), and histological verification (C177-C179). The outlier removal procedure (C162-C163) is reasonable (2.5% of trials removed). The methods are generally rigorous, though some details about the bootstrapping procedure (C59) could be more explicit.
